title: Measuring Pull and Push in Plants
endLine: Gas balances xylem tension; probes and stylets tap positive phloem pressure.

scenes.tts: How do you measure opposite pressures inside a living stem? Evaporation pulls water up dead xylem pipes under tension, below zero. Living phloem tubes push sugar sap under positive pressure.
scenes.caption: How do you measure opposite pressures inside a living stem? Evaporation pulls water up dead xylem pipes under tension, below zero. Living phloem tubes push sugar sap under positive pressure.
scenes.visual: Carried world, filling over 60% of frame height: a schematic cross-section of one leafy plant stem with two side-by-side conduits and a vertical pressure gauge (schematic, 0 in middle, negative below, positive above). On the opening question, a question mark pulses over both hidden conduits. Left conduit (dead hollow xylem, blue) pulls water upward as mist evaporates from the leaf and the xylem marker drops below zero (Tension < 0). Right conduit (living phloem sieve tubes with perforated sieve plates, amber) pushes sap downward from the leaf as its marker rises above zero (Pressure > 0). Continuous gentle particle drift in both tubes; no molecular structures.
scenes.narration: How do you measure opposite pressures inside a living stem? Evaporation pulls water up dead xylem pipes under tension, below zero. Living phloem tubes push sugar sap under positive pressure.

scenes.visual: The carried leafy stem fades slightly into the background with gentle ambient sap drift while the title card 'Measuring Pull and Push in Plants' sits cleanly centered at high contrast for 2 seconds.

scenes.tts: Start with xylem tension. Seal a cut leaf in a steel Scholander pressure chamber. Raise gas pressure until sap just appears at the cut. That pressure balances the xylem's tension. So the shoot's water potential, water's energy relative to pure water, is roughly minus that pressure.
scenes.caption: Start with xylem tension. Seal a cut leaf in a steel Scholander pressure chamber. Raise gas pressure until sap just appears at the cut. That pressure balances the xylem's tension. So the shoot's water potential, water's energy relative to pure water, is roughly minus that pressure.
scenes.visual: Zoom onto the leaf at the top of the carried stem while the pressure gauge stays on screen (schematic). A clean cut detaches the leaf; the blue xylem water sits just below the cut surface (schematic). A cutaway steel Scholander pressure chamber closes around the leaf with the cut stem poking through a top seal. Gas arrows swirl inside as a gas-pressure dial climbs steadily; the blue sap rises to the cut surface and beads right at the edge. The gas dial freezes at that balance point and its value mirrors, with a minus sign written in as spoken, onto the negative side of the gauge ('Water potential ≈ − balancing pressure').
scenes.narration: Start with xylem tension. Seal a cut leaf in a steel Scholander pressure chamber. Raise gas pressure until sap just appears at the cut. That pressure balances the xylem's tension. So the shoot's water potential, water's energy relative to pure water, is roughly minus that pressure.

scenes.tts: Now phloem: its sieve tubes, chains of living cells, carry sugar. An aphid pushes its thin mouthpart, a stylet, into one sieve tube. Cut the aphid away, leaving only the open stylet. Does sap pull back inside, stop, or keep oozing out?
scenes.caption: Now phloem: its sieve tubes, chains of living cells, carry sugar. An aphid pushes its thin mouthpart, a stylet, into one sieve tube. Cut the aphid away, leaving only the open stylet. Does sap pull back inside, stop, or keep oozing out?
scenes.visual: Pan right across the same stem cross-section to zoom into the living amber phloem sieve tubes (chained cells with perforated sieve plates; schematic). A small silhouette of an aphid lands on the stem exterior and slides its needle-thin mouthpart ('Stylet') straight into one sieve tube. Scissors snip the aphid body away, leaving only the hollow stylet embedded in the tube wall. At the open tip of the stylet, three short arrow prompts appear beside a question banner: 'Pulls back?', 'Stops?', or 'Oozes out?'.
scenes.narration: Now phloem: its sieve tubes, chains of living cells, carry sugar. An aphid pushes its thin mouthpart, a stylet, into one sieve tube. Cut the aphid away, leaving only the open stylet. Does sap pull back inside, stop, or keep oozing out?

scenes.visual: Hold the severed stylet embedded in the sieve tube with the question 'Pulls back, stops, or oozes out?' on screen for 4.5 seconds while a calm progress bar ticks across the bottom.

scenes.tts: Sap keeps oozing, pushed out by positive pressure inside the sieve tube. The ooze is nearly pure phloem sap. To measure that pressure, called turgor, a glass pico-gauge enters one living sieve tube. Its tip holds a tiny trapped volume of oil. How far sap squeezes the oil reads the pressure inside one working cell.
scenes.caption: Sap keeps oozing, pushed out by positive pressure inside the sieve tube. The ooze is nearly pure phloem sap. To measure that pressure, called turgor, a glass pico-gauge enters one living sieve tube. Its tip holds a tiny trapped volume of oil. How far sap squeezes the oil reads the pressure inside one working cell.
scenes.visual: The 'Oozes out' arrow lights up as amber droplets steadily bead and drip from the open stylet tip, lifting the carried gauge into positive territory ('Turgor > 0', schematic). Next along the same sieve tube, a tapered glass tip ('Pico-gauge') glides into the living cell; inside the glass tip is a clearly bounded pocket of trapped clear oil. Amber sap pushes inward against the oil meniscus, compressing the oil pocket; a bracket measures the compression distance and updates the positive turgor readout on the carried gauge.
scenes.narration: Sap keeps oozing, pushed out by positive pressure inside the sieve tube. The ooze is nearly pure phloem sap. To measure that pressure, called turgor, a glass pico-gauge enters one living sieve tube. Its tip holds a tiny trapped volume of oil. How far sap squeezes the oil reads the pressure inside one working cell.

scenes.tts: Pressure alone does not give flow speed. Feed a leaf carbon dioxide labelled with radioactive carbon eleven; it makes labelled sugar. Detectors along the stem time its arrival. Distance between detectors divided by travel time gives speed.
scenes.caption: Pressure alone does not give flow speed. Feed a leaf carbon dioxide labelled with radioactive carbon-11; it makes labelled sugar. Detectors along the stem time its arrival. Distance between detectors divided by travel time gives speed.
scenes.visual: Zoom out to the full carried leafy stem (schematic). Glowing pulse dots enter the top leaf ('Carbon-11', no molecular structures) and stream down the amber phloem conduit as a bright moving front. Two small detector rings mounted along the stem light up in sequence as a simple timer ticks between them; a bracket marks the distance between rings and 'speed = distance ÷ time' writes on screen as spoken (no numbers). As the summary is spoken, the frame holds both sides of the stem together: steel chamber balancing blue xylem tension on the left; pico-gauge and oozing stylet ('pressure') and glowing tracer pulse ('flow') along amber phloem on the right.
scenes.narration: Pressure alone does not give flow speed. Feed a leaf carbon dioxide labelled with radioactive carbon-11; it makes labelled sugar. Detectors along the stem time its arrival. Distance between detectors divided by travel time gives speed.

scenes.tts: Physiologists count embolisms, gas bubbles that break xylem water columns, to judge drought damage. But cutting a tense stem under water can itself create embolisms. X-ray microtomography merges angled X-ray images into three-dimensional stem scans. Air-filled and water-filled pipes look different, so scanning before and after cutting exposes false bubbles. Rehydrating first relaxes tension to test the cause.

Rehydrating first relaxes tension to test the cause.
scenes.visual: Return to the blue xylem pipes of the carried stem, submerged under a schematic water surface. A blade cuts the tense stem; bright pale gas bubbles ('Embolisms') suddenly snap open inside nearby vessels, breaking blue columns. An X-ray beam arc sweeps around an intact stem section, assembling a 3D cross-section where water-filled pipes appear dark blue and air-filled pipes appear bright white (schematic). A before-and-after wipe flags newly empty pipes as 'Cutting artifact'. Beside it, a rehydrated stem whose tension gauge rises close to zero stays mostly blue after the same cut.
scenes.narration: Physiologists count embolisms, gas bubbles that break xylem water columns, to judge drought damage. But cutting a tense stem under water can itself create embolisms. X-ray microtomography merges angled X-ray images into three-dimensional stem scans. Air-filled and water-filled pipes look different, so scanning before and after cutting exposes false bubbles. Rehydrating first relaxes tension to test the cause.

scenes.tts: Phloem measurements have limits too. In one key study, pressure at the root end came from root cortex cells, not sieve tubes. So the real pressure drop along the tubes may be smaller. Its numbers hold for one species; oak data were removed during review.
scenes.caption: Phloem measurements have limits too. In one key study, pressure at the root end came from root cortex cells, not sieve tubes. So the real pressure drop along the tubes may be smaller. Its numbers hold for one species; oak data were removed during review.
scenes.visual: Pan down the carried plant to the root end (schematic). A glass probe approaches a narrow root sieve tube, then shifts to an adjacent larger cell labelled 'Root cortex proxy'. On the carried pressure gauge, the top-to-root pressure-drop bar brackets a dotted uncertainty band showing the true drop could be smaller. Beside the stem, a small tag 'Oak' fades and lifts off the notebook panel, leaving only 'Morning glory' highlighted while a tall tree silhouette sits dimmed with 'Untested'.
scenes.narration: Phloem measurements have limits too. In one key study, pressure at the root end came from root cortex cells, not sieve tubes. So the real pressure drop along the tubes may be smaller. Its numbers hold for one species; oak data were removed during review.

scenes.tts: These tools unlocked two results. In 2015, Torres-Ruiz and colleagues found that cutting under water while xylem was under tension itself created embolisms. It occurred in four species, varying with species and tension. So counts from cut stems can overstate drought damage.
scenes.caption: These tools unlocked two results. In 2015, Torres-Ruiz and colleagues found that cutting under water while xylem was under tension itself created embolisms. It occurred in four species, varying with species and tension. So counts from cut stems can overstate drought damage.
scenes.visual: Left side of the carried world highlights the xylem X-ray scan panel tagged 'Torres-Ruiz and colleagues, 2015'. An intact 3D stem cross-section with mostly blue water-filled conduits transforms after an underwater cut under tension, flashing white air-filled bubbles across several conduits (schematic). Four small species tags appear in a row, each with a different number of new bubbles (schematic). A tally labelled 'cut-stem count' sits above the true count, marked 'overstated'.
scenes.narration: These tools unlocked two results. In 2015, Torres-Ruiz and colleagues found that cutting under water while xylem was under tension itself created embolisms. It occurred in four species, varying with species and tension. So counts from cut stems can overstate drought damage.

scenes.tts: In 2016, Knoblauch, Holbrook and colleagues tested Münch's 1930 idea in morning glory. Münch proposed that sugar loaded at a source leaf raises pressure, pushing sap toward where sugar is used. Critics argued long, narrow sieve tubes would need more pressure than living cells could hold. So the team lengthened vines.
scenes.caption: In 2016, Knoblauch, Holbrook and colleagues tested Münch's 1930 idea in morning glory. scenes.visual: Right side of the carried world extends the leafy stem into a morning glory vine tagged 'Knoblauch, Holbrook and colleagues, 2016 (Münch, 1930)'. On Münch's idea, sugar dots load at the source leaf and pressure arrows push sap toward a root. On the critics' doubt, a long, narrow amber sieve tube shows a pressure gauge straining with a question mark (schematic). The vine then grows visibly longer.
scenes.narration: In 2016, Knoblauch, Holbrook and colleagues tested Münch's 1930 idea in morning glory. scenes.tts: Source turgor rose from about zero point seven five to more than two point two megapascals. Sieve tubes also conducted five to six times better. Together, pressure flow's estimated reach matched the vine's length.
scenes.caption: Source turgor rose from about 0.75 to more than 2.2 MPa. Sieve tubes also conducted five to six times better. Together, pressure flow's estimated reach matched the vine's length.
scenes.visual: Along a pressure bar (0 to more than 2.2 MPa; small callout '1 MPa ≈ 10 atmospheres'), the source turgor level climbs from 0.75 MPa in a short young vine to above 2.2 MPa in the longest vine, while the amber sieve tube widens to show five- to six-fold higher conductivity (schematic). On the last sentence a 'reach' bracket stretches from the source leaf to meet the vine's tip.
scenes.narration: Source turgor rose from about 0.75 to more than 2.2 MPa. Sieve tubes also conducted five to six times better. Together, pressure flow's estimated reach matched the vine's length.
